title: Dynamic Programming
tagline: The technique that transforms exponential brute-force into polynomial solutions by never solving the same subproblem twice.

sections.content:
Dynamic programming (DP) is one of the most powerful and widely misunderstood ideas in all of computer science. It is not a single algorithm — it is a **design paradigm**, a way of structuring computation that applies whenever a problem can be decomposed into overlapping subproblems whose results combine to form the overall solution. Once you learn to recognise the pattern, problems that appeared to require exponential search collapse to polynomial time solutions that execute in milliseconds.

The name itself is misleading. Richard Bellman coined 'dynamic programming' in the 1950s while working at RAND Corporation, deliberately choosing a vague and impressive-sounding term to hide the mathematical nature of his research from his government sponsors who were suspicious of the word 'mathematics'. The technique has nothing to do with 'dynamic' in the sense of runtime dynamism, and 'programming' referred to planning (as in linear programming) not code. Do not let the name confuse you — the concept is fundamentally about **remembering answers to avoid recomputation**.

DP problems share two hallmarks: **overlapping subproblems** (the same sub-computation is needed many times across the solution space) and **optimal substructure** (the optimal solution to the whole problem is composed of optimal solutions to its subproblems). When both properties hold, you can break the problem into pieces, solve each piece once, store the result, and build upward. The canonical examples — Fibonacci numbers, coin change, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, matrix chain multiplication — recur endlessly in technical interviews, compilers, route planners, bioinformatics, and financial modelling.

This chapter builds a complete mental model: what DP is and why it works, the two implementation strategies (memoisation and tabulation), how to identify DP problems and derive recurrences, worked examples of increasing complexity, space optimisation tricks, and common failure modes. By the end you will be able to approach an unfamiliar DP problem with a repeatable, systematic method.

sections.title: The Notebook on the Staircase
sections.content:
Imagine you are counting the distinct ways to climb n stairs, taking either 1 or 2 steps at a time. A naïve approach tries every path recursively: from stair n you could have come from stair n-1 (one step back) or stair n-2 (two steps back), so you recurse on both. For stair 40 this fans out into millions of redundant calls — `ways(38)` gets computed by `ways(40)`, `ways(39)`, and `ways(38)` independently, and each of those re-triggers the same avalanche of sub-calls below.

Now bring a notepad and tape it to the wall. The first time you compute 'ways to reach stair k', you write the answer in the notepad next to 'stair k'. Every subsequent call for stair k takes one glance at the notepad instead of recursing. This is **memoisation** — the memo table is the key insight, not the recursion.

The alternative: start from stair 0 and fill the notepad left-to-right before you ever need a lookup. `ways(0)=1`, `ways(1)=1`, `ways(2)=ways(1)+ways(0)=2`, `ways(3)=ways(2)+ways(1)=3` — you never recurse at all. This is **tabulation**. Both strategies eliminate redundancy; they differ only in direction. Memoisation is top-down (start at the goal, recurse, cache lazily). Tabulation is bottom-up (start at the base cases, build upward eagerly). The complexity improvement is identical — what changes is which subproblems get computed and in which order.

sections.title: The Two Hallmarks: Overlapping Subproblems
sections.content:
**Overlapping subproblems** is the defining characteristic that separates DP from plain divide-and-conquer. In merge sort, you split the array in half and recurse — but the two halves never share work. In Fibonacci, `fib(5)` calls `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`, but `fib(4)` also calls `fib(3)` — the `fib(3)` subtree is computed twice. Two levels down, `fib(3)` spawns `fib(2)` twice, and `fib(2)` spawns `fib(1)` twice each — the redundancy compounds exponentially. `fib(40)` requires over a billion naïve recursive calls; with memoisation it requires exactly 40.

The test for overlapping subproblems is simple: draw the recursion tree for a small input and look for repeated nodes. If the same function arguments appear at multiple nodes in the tree, the subproblems overlap and caching is worthwhile. If every node has unique arguments (like merge sort), there is nothing to cache and divide-and-conquer is fine without DP.

Memoisation (top-down DP) attaches a cache to the recursion: before computing `fib(n)`, check if the answer is already in the cache; if so, return it immediately. The call tree is still explored depth-first, but already-computed branches are pruned to a single lookup. Each value from `fib(0)` to `fib(n)` is computed exactly once — O(n) total work instead of O(2ⁿ).

sections.title: The Two Hallmarks: Optimal Substructure
sections.content:
**Optimal substructure** means the globally optimal solution is composed of optimal solutions to its subproblems. This sounds abstract, but it is the reason DP can produce correct answers — not just fast ones. Without optimal substructure, finding the local optimum for a subproblem tells you nothing about the global optimum, and DP would produce wrong answers.

Coin change is the clearest example. The problem: given coins of various denominations, what is the minimum number of coins that sum to amount W? Define `dp[w]` as the minimum coins needed to make amount w. The recurrence is `dp[w] = 1 + min(dp[w - coin])` for all coins ≤ w. Why is this correct? Because if the optimal solution for amount w uses a particular last coin c, then the remaining amount `w - c` must also be solved optimally — if there were a better way to make `w - c`, we could substitute it and improve the solution for w. That substitution argument is optimal substructure in action.

Contrast with the **longest simple path** in a general graph (with cycles). The longest simple path does NOT have optimal substructure: the longest simple path from A to C passing through B is not necessarily composed of the longest simple path from A to B and the longest from B to C, because the sub-paths might share vertices, violating the 'simple' (no repeated vertices) constraint. DP would give wrong answers here. This is why recognising optimal substructure is crucial — DP is powerful but not universally applicable.

**Shortest path** (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) does have optimal substructure: any sub-path of a shortest path is itself a shortest path. This is why DP formulations underpin all shortest-path algorithms.

sections.title: Top-Down vs Bottom-Up: Two Routes to the Same Answer
sections.content:
Given a valid recurrence, you have two routes to implement it.

**Top-down (memoisation)** wraps an existing recursive solution with a cache. You write the recursion exactly as the recurrence says — the base case returns directly, the recursive case combines subproblem results — and add a `memo` Map (or array) keyed on the function arguments. Before computing, check the cache; before returning, store in the cache. This approach computes only the subproblems that are actually needed, which is beneficial when the subproblem space is sparse (only a fraction of all possible subproblems are reachable from the top). It is also often easier to derive correctly because the recursion directly mirrors the recurrence relation.

**Bottom-up (tabulation)** iterates from the smallest subproblems upward, filling a table. You must determine the correct iteration order — subproblems must be solved before any problem that depends on them. For 1D recurrences like Fibonacci or coin change, this is simply left-to-right. For 2D recurrences like LCS or knapsack, you iterate over rows then columns (or the reverse, depending on dependency direction). Tabulation has no recursion overhead, better CPU cache locality (iterating an array sequentially is hardware-friendly), and no risk of stack overflow for large inputs. In practice, tabulation is usually 2–5× faster in wall-clock time even at the same asymptotic complexity.

A practical rule of thumb: **derive the recurrence top-down (it is easier to think recursively), then implement bottom-up (it is faster and safer).** Many competitive programmers and interview candidates write the memoised version first to verify correctness, then convert to tabulation for performance.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: fibNaive recomputes fib(3) exponentially many times for large n. fibMemo fixes this with a Map cache — each value fib(0)..fib(n) is computed exactly once, reducing time to O(n). fibTab eliminates recursion entirely by filling an array from index 0 upward. fibOpt observes that each step only needs the previous two values, so we can discard the array and use two rolling variables — the space drops from O(n) to O(1). This space optimisation pattern appears in many DP problems: when a row only depends on the immediately preceding row, you can fold the 2D table into a 1D array.

sections.title: Deriving a Recurrence: The Four-Step Method
sections.content:
The hardest part of DP is not implementing it — it is identifying that DP applies and then writing a correct recurrence. Here is a repeatable four-step method:

**Step 1: Define the subproblem state.** Express `dp[state]` in plain English. The state should capture everything you need to solve the subproblem independently of how you arrived at it. For coin change: `dp[w]` = minimum number of coins to make amount w. For 0/1 knapsack: `dp[i][w]` = maximum value using the first i items with capacity w. The state definition is the intellectual core of every DP solution.

**Step 2: Write the recurrence.** Express `dp[state]` in terms of smaller states. Ask: what is the last decision made? For coin change, the last coin used was some coin c, so the remaining problem is making amount `w - c`. For knapsack, the last decision is whether to include item i or not. The recurrence follows from enumerating those choices.

**Step 3: Identify base cases.** What states are trivially solvable without recursion? For coin change: `dp[0] = 0` (zero coins to make amount zero). For knapsack: `dp[0][w] = 0` for all w (no items means zero value). Base cases are the foundation — errors here propagate everywhere.

**Step 4: Determine iteration order.** For tabulation, ensure every subproblem you depend on is computed before you need it. For 1D recurrences this is usually left-to-right. For 2D recurrences, think about which quadrant of the table is filled first.

sections.title: Coin Change: A Worked Recurrence Derivation
sections.content:
**Problem:** Given coin denominations and a target amount W, find the minimum number of coins that sum to W. Return -1 if impossible.

**Step 1 — State:** `dp[w]` = minimum coins to make amount w exactly.

**Step 2 — Recurrence:** The last coin used must be some denomination c where c ≤ w. After using coin c, we need to make amount `w - c` optimally. So: `dp[w] = 1 + min(dp[w - c])` over all coins c ≤ w. We try every applicable coin and take the minimum over all choices.

**Step 3 — Base cases:** `dp[0] = 0` (amount zero needs zero coins). `dp[w] = Infinity` initially for all w > 0, representing 'impossible' — any reachable amount will be updated below Infinity.

**Step 4 — Iteration order:** Left-to-right, w from 1 to W. When computing `dp[w]`, all `dp[w - c]` have smaller indices and are already computed.

This is the **unbounded knapsack** structure — each coin denomination can be used any number of times. Compare this to 0/1 knapsack where each item can be used at most once, which requires a different iteration strategy.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The inner loop tries every coin denomination for each amount w. The key line `dp[w - coin] + 1` reads: 'if we use this coin, the cost is 1 plus the optimal cost for the remaining amount'. We keep the minimum over all valid coins. The greedy example (coins=[1,3,4], amount=6) demonstrates why DP is necessary — greedy algorithms fail on non-canonical coin systems, making DP the only correct general approach.

sections.caption: Coin change tabulation for coins [1,3,4]: dp[6]=2 via 3+3, not the greedy path of 4+1+1=3. DP explores all possibilities and keeps the minimum.

sections.title: 0/1 Knapsack: Two-Dimensional DP
sections.content:
The **0/1 knapsack** problem adds a constraint that makes the coin change approach fail: each item can be used **at most once**. Given n items each with a weight and a value, and a knapsack with capacity W, find the maximum value you can carry.

**Step 1 — State:** `dp[i][w]` = maximum value achievable using the **first i items** with weight capacity exactly **at most w**.

**Step 2 — Recurrence:** For each item i, you make a binary choice:
- **Skip item i:** `dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]` — the value is the same as without item i.
- **Take item i** (only if `weight[i] ≤ w`): `dp[i][w] = value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]` — you gain the item's value and use up some capacity.
- Final: `dp[i][w] = max(skip, take)` when item fits; `dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]` when it does not.

**Why `i-1` for item i?** This is the key insight. When deciding about item i, you consult the table row for `i-1` — the state before item i was considered. This ensures item i is counted at most once. The 2D table naturally enforces the 0/1 constraint.

**Space optimisation:** Since `dp[i][w]` only depends on row `i-1`, you can fold the 2D table into a single 1D array by iterating the capacity dimension **right-to-left**. Iterating left-to-right would mean `dp[w - weight[i]]` has already been updated to include item i in the current pass — effectively using item i multiple times (unbounded knapsack). Right-to-left preserves the 'previous row' semantics.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The 2D version makes the recurrence transparent: dp[i][w] is computed from the previous row dp[i-1]. The space-optimised 1D version is identical in logic but reuses a single array. The critical detail is the right-to-left inner loop — when processing capacity w and looking back at dp[w - weight[i]], the right-to-left direction guarantees that index has not yet been updated in this pass (it still holds the 'previous item' value). Reversing to left-to-right silently turns the problem into unbounded knapsack.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["dp[i][w] decision"] --> B{"weight[i] > w?"}
    B -- Yes --> C["dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]\n(skip, item too heavy)"]
    B -- No --> D["skip = dp[i-1][w]"]
    D --> E["take = value[i] + dp[i-1][w-weight[i]]"]
    E --> F["dp[i][w] = max(skip, take)"]
sections.caption: 0/1 Knapsack decision tree per cell: if item fits, compare taking vs skipping. Both branches read from row i-1, enforcing the at-most-once constraint.

sections.title: Longest Common Subsequence: Sequence DP
sections.content:
The **Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)** problem asks: given two strings (or arrays), what is the length of the longest sequence that appears in both, in order, but not necessarily contiguously? LCS underlies `diff` tools (like `git diff`), DNA sequence alignment in bioinformatics, and plagiarism detection.

**State:** `dp[i][j]` = length of LCS of the first i characters of string A and the first j characters of string B.

**Recurrence:** There are two cases:
- If `A[i-1] === B[j-1]` (characters match): the LCS can include this character, so `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]`.
- If characters do not match: we skip either A's character or B's character, taking the better option: `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.

**Base cases:** `dp[0][j] = 0` for all j (empty string A has no common chars with any string), `dp[i][0] = 0` for all i.

**Intuition:** When characters match at positions i and j, we know they form part of the LCS. We 'consume' both and look at the LCS of everything before them. When they do not match, one of them is not part of the LCS extension — we try both possibilities and take the maximum.

This 2D structure is also used in **edit distance** (Levenshtein distance), which computes the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions to transform one string into another. Edit distance underlies spell checkers, fuzzy search, and DNA alignment tools.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["A = ABCBDAB"] --> B["B = BDCAB"]
    B --> C["LCS = BCAB\nlength 4"]
    C --> D["dp table\n8x6 cells"]
    D --> E["dp[i][j]:\nmatch → dp[i-1][j-1]+1\nno match → max(dp[i-1][j],dp[i][j-1])"]
sections.caption: LCS of ABCBDAB and BDCAB is BCAB (length 4). The 2D dp table is filled row by row; each cell depends only on the cell diagonally above-left (match) or above/left (no match).

sections.title: Identifying DP Problems in the Wild
sections.content:
The ability to recognise DP opportunity in an unfamiliar problem is the true skill. Here are the reliable signals:

**Signal 1: 'Count the number of ways...'** — These problems almost always have overlapping subproblems. Counting distinct paths on a grid, counting ways to make change, counting valid parenthesizations. The recurrence sums subproblem counts rather than taking a minimum or maximum.

**Signal 2: 'Find the minimum/maximum...' with a search space that seems combinatorial** — If brute force explores exponentially many possibilities (subsets, sequences, partitions), DP likely applies. Coin change (min coins), knapsack (max value), shortest path in weighted graphs.

**Signal 3: 'Yes/no feasibility with constraints'** — Can you reach the target sum? Can you partition the array? Is the string a valid encoding? These Boolean DP problems use `dp[state] = true/false` and OR-combine subproblem results.

**Signal 4: Sequence problems** — Anything involving two sequences (LCS, edit distance, sequence alignment) or one sequence with a range (longest palindromic subsequence, matrix chain multiplication) typically has a 2D DP formulation.

**Anti-signal: Greedy works.** If you can prove that always taking the locally optimal choice leads to the global optimum (e.g., activity selection, Huffman coding), use greedy — it is simpler and faster. DP is for problems where greedy fails because earlier choices affect future options in complex, non-local ways.

**Anti-signal: No overlapping subproblems.** Merge sort, binary search, and most divide-and-conquer algorithms partition the problem into non-overlapping halves. DP overhead would be wasted here.

**Historical context:** Richard Bellman developed dynamic programming in the 1950s while working on multistage decision problems at RAND. The Bellman equation — a recurrence expressing the optimal value of a sequential decision process — is the foundation of modern reinforcement learning. Bellman-Ford shortest path, policy evaluation in Markov Decision Processes, and Q-learning in deep RL all apply the same principle: define a value function over states, express it recursively, solve iteratively. When you study DP for interviews, you are learning the same mathematics that trains game-playing AI agents.

sections.title: Common DP Patterns and Their Recurrences
sections.content:
DP problems cluster into recognisable patterns. Memorising the pattern lets you adapt rather than re-derive from scratch:

**Linear sequence DP** — `dp[i]` depends on a fixed number of previous entries. Fibonacci, climbing stairs, house robber (no adjacent houses), maximum subarray (Kadane's algorithm). These are O(n) time.

**Two-sequence DP** — `dp[i][j]` where i indexes one sequence and j indexes another. LCS, edit distance, interleaving strings. These are O(m × n) time and space, often optimisable to O(min(m,n)) space.

**Knapsack variants** — A set of items and a capacity constraint:
- 0/1 knapsack: items used at most once → right-to-left inner loop.
- Unbounded knapsack (coin change): items used any number of times → left-to-right inner loop.
- Bounded knapsack: each item has a quantity limit → requires additional logic.

**Interval DP** — `dp[i][j]` represents the optimal solution for the sub-sequence or sub-array from index i to j. Matrix chain multiplication, optimal BST, burst balloons. These are O(n³) time — the outer loop iterates over interval lengths.

**Bitmask DP** — state includes a bitmask of which items have been selected. Travelling salesman problem (TSP) on small graphs, counting Hamiltonian paths. These are O(2ⁿ × n) — exponential but much better than O(n!) brute force.

**Tree DP** — dp defined on tree nodes, combining child subtree values. Maximum independent set on a tree, diameter of a tree. These are O(n) time using DFS post-order.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: House Robber is a linear-sequence DP — the decision at each house is to rob it (gain its value, skip the previous) or skip it (keep previous maximum). Space-optimised to O(1) by keeping only prev1 and prev2. LIS is O(n²): for each position i, scan all earlier positions j where nums[j] < nums[i] and extend those subsequences. countSubsets uses the 0/1 knapsack pattern (right-to-left inner loop) but counts ways instead of maximising value — notice dp[0]=1 as base case (one way to reach sum 0) instead of dp[0]=0.

sections.title: Space Optimisation Techniques
sections.content:
A DP solution is not complete until you have considered space optimisation. Many 2D DP problems can be reduced to 1D, and many 1D problems to O(1).

**Rolling array (1D ← 2D):** When `dp[i][w]` only depends on `dp[i-1][...]`, you do not need to keep the full 2D table — only the previous row. Replace `dp[i-1]` with a 1D array and overwrite it in the correct direction for the current row. This is the technique used for 0/1 knapsack (right-to-left) and LCS (requires slightly more care with a temporary variable or two alternating arrays).

**Two-variable sliding (O(1) ← O(n)):** When `dp[i]` depends only on `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]` (like Fibonacci, climbing stairs, house robber), replace the array with two scalar variables. Update them as you iterate.

**Observation:** Space optimisation never changes time complexity — it only reduces memory. The asymptotic time is determined by the number of subproblems and the work per subproblem. Focus on getting the algorithm correct first, then apply space optimisation as a final step.

**Trade-off alert:** Space-optimised versions are harder to reconstruct the actual solution (not just the optimal value) from. If you need to output the optimal items chosen (not just the maximum value), you typically need the full table or a separate backtracking pass. In interviews, clarify whether you need the value or the actual solution path.

**Interview strategy — the five-step DP template:**
1. **Recognise** the problem type (count ways / find min-max / yes-no feasibility).
2. **Define** the subproblem state in one English sentence before writing any code.
3. **Write the recurrence** by asking 'what is the last choice made?' and enumerating all options.
4. **Identify base cases** — states that can be answered without the recurrence.
5. **Code** top-down with memoisation first (easier to get right), then convert to bottom-up if asked to optimise.

**Common mistakes to avoid:** Forgetting to initialise impossible states to Infinity (coin change) or 0 (count problems) leads to silent wrong answers. Iterating the 0/1 knapsack inner loop left-to-right instead of right-to-left converts it to unbounded knapsack — the code looks correct but gives wrong answers for duplicate items. Off-by-one errors in the recurrence (using `nums[i]` vs `nums[i-1]` in 1-indexed vs 0-indexed tables) are the single most common source of bugs. Always trace through a small example manually before submitting.

items: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has **overlapping subproblems** (the same sub-computation is needed repeatedly) and **optimal substructure** (the globally optimal solution is composed of optimal subproblem solutions). Both properties must hold.

**Memoisation (top-down)**: attach a cache to a recursive solution — each subproblem is computed once and stored. Easier to derive from a recursive definition; computes only needed subproblems. Risk: stack overflow on large inputs.

**Tabulation (bottom-up)**: fill a dp table iteratively from base cases upward. No recursion overhead, better cache locality, no stack risk. Often 2–5× faster in practice at the same asymptotic complexity.

The **four-step derivation method**: (1) define dp[state] in English, (2) write the recurrence by enumerating last-choice options, (3) identify base cases, (4) determine iteration order. Nail the recurrence first — the code follows mechanically.

**0/1 knapsack inner loop direction is critical**: right-to-left enforces each item used at most once (0/1); left-to-right allows unlimited reuse (unbounded/coin change). This single loop direction change switches between two fundamentally different problems.

Common DP patterns cluster into: linear sequence (house robber, LIS), two-sequence (LCS, edit distance), knapsack variants (0/1, unbounded, bounded), interval DP (matrix chain), and bitmask DP (TSP). Recognising the pattern accelerates solution design.

**Space optimisation**: 2D tables often fold to 1D arrays (rolling row technique); 1D arrays with two-value dependencies fold to two scalar variables. Space optimisation never changes time complexity — apply after correctness is confirmed.

quiz.question: What are the two properties that identify a problem as solvable by dynamic programming?
options: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Sorted input and divide-and-conquer structure
Linear time complexity and constant space
quiz.explanation: DP requires overlapping subproblems (the same subcomputation is needed many times, making caching worthwhile) and optimal substructure (the optimal solution to the problem uses optimal solutions to its subproblems, enabling composition). Greedy problems only need optimal substructure and the greedy choice property.

quiz.question: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci O(2^n) while memoised Fibonacci is O(n)?
options: Memoisation uses an iterative loop instead of recursion
Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially; memoisation computes each of the n+1 subproblems exactly once
Memoisation sorts the recursive calls before executing them
Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially so naive computation is inherently exponential
quiz.explanation: Each call to fib(n) branches into fib(n-1) and fib(n-2) without caching. fib(n-2) is recomputed by multiple branches — exponential redundancy results. Memoisation stores each fib(k) after first computing it; subsequent calls return the cached value. Total distinct subproblems: n+1, each computed once — O(n) time.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between memoisation (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) DP?
options: Memoisation always uses more memory than tabulation
Memoisation starts from the goal and recurses lazily caching results; tabulation iterates from base cases upward filling a table eagerly
Tabulation is only applicable to 1D problems; memoisation works on any dimension
They have different asymptotic time complexity
quiz.explanation: Both eliminate redundant computation. Memoisation is top-down: it recurses from the goal state, computing subproblems only when needed (lazy), caching each result. Tabulation is bottom-up: it iterates from base cases, filling every subproblem in dependency order (eager). Asymptotic complexity is the same; tabulation avoids recursion overhead, stack limits, and has better cache locality.

quiz.question: In coin change tabulation `dp[w] = 1 + min(dp[w - coin])`, why is `dp[0] = 0` the correct base case?
options: It is a sentinel representing that amount 0 is impossible
Amount 0 requires exactly 0 coins — it is the foundation all other dp[w] values build upon
It represents using a coin of denomination 0
It prevents array index out-of-bounds when w equals a coin value
quiz.explanation: Making amount 0 requires 0 coins — this is trivially true and forms the base case. dp[coin] = 1 + dp[0] = 1, meaning one coin of that denomination makes the target. Without dp[0]=0, the recurrence has no foundation and all values would incorrectly remain Infinity.

quiz.question: Why does 0/1 knapsack iterate the capacity dimension right-to-left when using a 1D dp array?
options: To improve cache performance by accessing memory in reverse order
Right-to-left ensures dp[w - weight[i]] still reflects the pre-item-i state, enforcing that each item is counted at most once
To handle items whose weight is larger than half the capacity
Because the recurrence is only valid when capacity decreases
quiz.explanation: With a 1D array, iterating left-to-right would mean dp[w - weight[i]] has already been updated with item i in the current pass — item i could be added multiple times, turning 0/1 knapsack into unbounded knapsack. Iterating right-to-left guarantees dp[w - weight[i]] still holds the value from before item i was processed, enforcing at-most-once inclusion.

quiz.question: coinChange([1, 3, 4], 6) — what is the minimum number of coins, and why does greedy fail here?
options: 3 coins (4+1+1); greedy works fine here
2 coins (3+3); greedy picks 4 first leaving 2, which needs two 1s — giving 3 coins instead of 2
2 coins (4+2); greedy correctly identifies the pair
6 coins (six 1s); no efficient solution exists for this coin set
quiz.explanation: Greedy takes the largest coin that fits: 4 (remainder 2), then two 1s — total 3 coins. But 3+3=6 uses only 2 coins. Greedy fails because choosing 4 first blocks the optimal 3+3 path. DP considers all possible last coins at each amount and always finds the global minimum.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of the bottom-up coin change DP with amount W and k coin denominations?
options: O(W)
O(k × W)
O(k log W)
quiz.explanation: The outer loop runs W times (amounts 1 to W). The inner loop runs k times per amount (once per coin denomination). Total work: O(k × W). This is pseudo-polynomial — polynomial in the numeric value of W, but exponential in the bit-length of W. In practice this is efficient for typical coin change inputs.

quiz.question: In the LCS recurrence, when characters A[i-1] and B[j-1] DO match, what is dp[i][j]?
options: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
quiz.explanation: When the characters match, they can both be included in the LCS. We extend the LCS of the strings before these positions (dp[i-1][j-1]) by 1. When they do not match, one character must be skipped — we take the better of skipping A's character (dp[i-1][j]) or skipping B's character (dp[i][j-1]).

quiz.question: Which problem does NOT have optimal substructure, making standard DP inapplicable?
options: Longest common subsequence of two strings
Shortest path in a weighted DAG
Longest simple path in a general graph with cycles
0/1 Knapsack with integer weights
quiz.explanation: Shortest paths and LCS have optimal substructure — sub-solutions of optimal solutions are themselves optimal. The longest simple path (no repeated vertices) does not: sub-paths of a globally longest simple path may not be locally longest simple paths, because avoiding vertex repetition creates global constraints that break local composability. DP would produce incorrect results.

quiz.question: What is the recommended interview strategy for deriving a DP solution under time pressure?
options: Start by filling in the tabulation table immediately — derive the code before the recurrence
Define dp[state] in English first, write the recurrence by asking 'what is the last choice?', identify base cases, then code top-down with memoisation
Draw the full state machine and all transitions before writing any code
Try greedy first — only switch to DP if the greedy answer is provably wrong
quiz.explanation: Defining the state clearly in English is the most important step — it forces you to understand what you are computing before you compute it. Writing the recurrence by asking 'what is the last decision made?' is a reliable technique. Top-down memoisation is easier to get correct under pressure because the recursion directly mirrors the recurrence. Tabulation can be derived from the same recurrence once correctness is confirmed.
